content.text:
In the opening pages of "To Kill a Mockingbird," Harper Lee establishes Scout's first-person perspective and introduces the Finch family history with the following excerpt:

“I maintain that the whole business began the summer old Miss Lorna came to stay with the Hartwells next door. Joshua said it began long before that. He said it began the summer Arnold came to us, when Arnold first gave us the idea of making Mr. Ridley come out.

I said if he wanted to take a broad view of the thing, it really began with Sherman Jackson, who in 1832 failed to surrender to Andrew Jackson at the battle of Horseshoe Bend, which was a pity because we were related to him on our mother's side. Joshua, who was a reader of histories, said that our Jackson had nothing to do with the general Jackson, and that the only connection between the two was that our Jackson had run a ferry on the Alabama river in 1813, where the general's men had crossed once with Creek scouts. Joshua said the ferry made our family more eccentric, not more distinguished, but I did not mind. Eccentric…”

This passage provides a rich basis for close reading, as it captures Scout's voice, her perspective on family history, and the blend of innocence and complex ideas that characterizes her narrative throughout the novel.
